title: Stable global economy over an extended period
setup: No event. Nine countries, eleven production zones, all governments on the fiscal autopilot, 20 simulated years.

indicators.label: World real GDP growth
indicators.note: technology trend plus catch-up of poorer zones

indicators.label: Worst conservation error
indicators.note: goods, money and bonds, every week

table.caption: World aggregates at the end of selected years

mechanisms: Firms plan output from smoothed sales, stock cover and price/cost margins; households spend a share of expected income; prices adjust to inventory gaps; wages follow unemployment and inflation.
The world monetary rule creates just enough money for real growth plus 2% inflation, so prices drift slowly while money, GDP and debt grow together instead of diverging.
Autopilot governments keep budgets near balance, so debt/GDP drifts to a comfortable level rather than exploding or vanishing.

checks.name: Real GDP grows (no stagnation or collapse)
Inflation stays moderate
No sovereign default or regime change without a shock
Debt ratios stay bounded
Conservation holds every week

title: Oil embargo between several countries
setup: Weeks 53-156: Khazir and Halcyon (energy exporters) forbid energy exports to Norland and Ostmark (importers). The embargo is lifted in week 157.

indicators.label: Energy supplied to targets by other countries
Real GDP of targets during embargo
Real GDP of exporters during embargo
Third-country (Sundara) energy exports vs own supply

table.caption: Energy price paid and real GDP relative to the control run

mechanisms: Sanctions are enforced on the physical flow: the embargoed pair is removed from the supplier list, so no energy moves between them whatever prices do.

Buyers automatically redirect orders to the next cheapest allowed suppliers; the delivered price (producer price + freight + tariff) decides the split, so the price rises by the extra freight and by the scarcity of non-embargoed supply.
Exporters lose their large customers, their stocks build up and local prices fall, which cuts revenue, profits and employment in the oil sector.
Energy is bought from producers' own stock, so a third country cannot launder embargoed oil: whatever it imports is consumed, buffered or turned into other goods, never re-sold.

checks.name: Embargo is strictly enforced (zero direct flow)
Trade is redirected to other suppliers
Targets pay more for energy
Exporters are hurt more than the world is
No laundering through a third country

title: Sudden 50% collapse of agricultural production in one country
setup: Week 53: the yield of Verdania's food sector (its main export) drops by 50% and recovers over 78 weeks.

indicators.label: Share of household food demand met (lowest)
Verdania export earnings (lowest, vs control)
indicators.note: a net food exporter: the shortfall falls on exports

indicators.label: Food price in Lirane (peak, vs control)
Weeks to return within 2% of control GDP

mechanisms: The shock lowers productivity, not employment: farms keep their workers but harvest half as much, so unit costs double and the sector's supply curve shifts left.

Verdania is a net food exporter, so the shortfall falls first on exports: domestic households are served from the reduced output (their fill stays near 100%) while export earnings, farm incomes and the trade balance take the hit; importers elsewhere pay more.
Lower farm income, higher food prices and a squeeze on other spending reduce living standards; stability falls, which can open an unrest episode.
Capacity is not destroyed, so as the yield recovers output returns and the economy converges back to the control path.

checks.name: Output falls by roughly half
Food gets more expensive locally
Exports fall while households stay supplied (the exporter absorbs the shock)
Society feels it (GDP down, stability down)
Economy recovers

title: Sharp increase in military expenditure
setup: Week 53: Ostmark (arms maker) raises military spending from 3.5% to 12% of GDP and keeps it there. The autopilot finances it with taxes.

indicators.label: Ostmark military equipment stock after 4 years
Ostmark military output
indicators.note: industry expands, with a construction delay

indicators.label: Income tax rate at the end
Household consumption in the last year
Real GDP in the last year

mechanisms: State orders for military goods (mostly industrial and military equipment) are added to private demand; the same factories, materials and workers are needed, so industrial prices rise and civilian buyers are crowded out.
Private firms respond to the higher margins by investing, but capacity takes about three quarters to build, so early output is limited by existing capacity and the build-up first shows as inflation.
The extra spending is paid with taxes and debt; higher taxes reduce household income, so consumption falls. A militarised economy is richer in weapons and poorer in everyday goods.

checks.name: Equipment stock grows markedly
Military industry expands
Consumption is crowded out
Industrial inputs get more expensive
The country pays with taxes and/or debt

title: War disrupting several international trade routes
setup: Weeks 53-156: the Strait of Kell, the east ocean route and the Halcyon sea lane become war zones (3x freight cost, 40% of normal throughput). Routes reopen in week 157.

indicators.label: Energy price in Sundara
indicators.note: importer cut off from the Gulf

indicators.label: World real GDP returns within 1% of control

mechanisms: A lane's effective length is distance × cost multiplier and its throughput caps flows. Trade follows the cheapest open path, so closing the strait pushes cargo to the long southern cape route automatically.
Freight costs rise on every affected pair, which lowers the delivered-price advantage of distant producers; buyers shift orders towards nearer suppliers and domestic output, shrinking total trade.

Countries whose only link to the world runs through the war zone lose revenue and employment and face shortages. Countries with alternative routes reroute or even gain: Khazir's rival exporter is cut off, so its overland customers pay more.

checks.name: World trade shrinks
The country whose only sea lane is cut loses far more than a diversified one
Prices rise for cut-off importers
Recovery after the routes reopen

title: Sovereign default by a major economy
setup: Part A: week 53: Norland (largest economy, debt 79% of GDP) declares default. Part B: Tavros (no autopilot) raises social, military and infrastructure spending to 50% of GDP in week 53 without raising taxes, to show a default emerging by itself.

indicators.label: A: loss borne by foreign creditors
A: Norland borrowing rate one week after
A: weeks until market access returns
A: Norland real GDP (lowest, vs control)
A: regime changes (defeat condition)
indicators.note: default alone does not end the player

indicators.label: A: world real GDP (lowest, vs control)
A: weeks to return within 2% of control GDP
A: Norland debt/GDP at the end
B: market access lost / forced default (week)
B: borrowing rate peak / debt-to-GDP peak
B: Tavros real GDP at the end (vs control)

table.caption: Part A - Norland relative to control

mechanisms: A default writes off a fixed share of the debt (provisional 55%). Because the engine records exactly who holds each country's bonds, the loss lands on those households, at home and abroad, reducing their wealth and spending.

The defaulter is shut out of credit markets for about 18 months (longer for repeat offenders) and carries a reputation premium that fades over three years; its government can only spend what it collects.

Financial disruption costs the economy a few percent of output for a year; stability takes a one-off hit. None of this is a defeat by itself: only a regime change, which needs a crisis episode to cross its thresholds, would end a human player.
Part B: when a deficit-running government is already near the market-access limit, interest costs and missed payments feed on each other until the forced default.

checks.name: Default writes off debt as designed
Foreign creditors lose money
Market access is lost, then restored
Output dips but the country survives and recovers
Stability falls after default
A default can emerge without any command

title: International coalition imposing economic sanctions
setup: Week 53: a five-country coalition (norland, sundara, verdania, halcyon, tavros) bans all trade with Ostmark in industrial goods, military equipment and raw materials, in both directions. Non-members keep trading.

indicators.label: Coalition ↔ Ostmark flow in sanctioned goods
Ostmark real GDP (from week 66, vs control)
Ostmark prices: industrial / military
indicators.note: export goods lose their markets, so they get cheaper at home

indicators.label: Coalition members' real GDP (mean)
indicators.note: sanctions are costly for senders too

mechanisms: Each member's ban is applied to the exact buyer-seller pair and good, in both directions, so every sanctioned flow disappears at the border of the transaction; there is no path through which goods can still arrive from a member.
Because goods are drawn from producers' own stock and never forwarded, a non-member that buys from Ostmark cannot resell those goods to a member as "its own": there is no re-export channel to close.
Ostmark must buy substitutes from non-members at higher delivered prices and sell its output to fewer, more distant buyers; its terms of trade worsen, margins shrink and employment falls.
Members pay too: they lose Ostmark's cheaper machinery and have to rebuy from other suppliers, so their prices rise slightly and the gap is partly captured by non-members.

checks.name: Sanctions are strictly enforced (no coalition ↔ Ostmark flow)
Ostmark is hurt
Trade is diverted to non-members
Senders bear some cost, much smaller than the target
Ostmark's terms of trade worsen (its export goods lose their markets and get cheaper at home)
Coalition buyers pay more for the goods they used to import

title: Small country heavily dependent on imports
setup: Lirane (6 million people, almost no energy, food or raw materials) is tested twice, with its 8-week strategic reserves usable and frozen. A: world energy supply falls 50% (Khazir and Halcyon) in week 53; Sundara (large, diversified) is the comparison. B: Lirane's only sea link is partly blockaded (2x freight cost, 50% of normal throughput) for 52 weeks.

indicators.label: A (world energy shock): consumption per head, 18 months
indicators.note: the same price rise hurts the large economy more: Lirane is rich per head, so basic needs absorb less of its budget (inferred from the model structure, not isolated by a separate run)

indicators.label: B: lowest share of household energy / food demand met
B: food / energy price paid in Lirane (peak)
B: Sundara consumption per head (unaffected route)

table.caption: B: Lirane under blockade (reserves usable) relative to control

mechanisms: An import-dependent economy has almost no domestic supply to fall back on and is a price-taker. A world price shock still passes through to it, but how much it hurts depends on the commodity's weight in the budget; in this run the rich-per-head island is hit less than the large poorer economy.

What truly exposes it is access: when its only sea link is restricted, supply (not just price) falls, households go short of necessities, its production chain loses inputs, and its high-wage, import-heavy structure makes the adjustment costly.

Strategic reserves are bought when prices are low and released automatically when prices or shortages cross thresholds. They buy time for the first months at the cost of tying up public money in stock.

checks.name: Lirane is far more import-dependent
A blockade hurts the island far more than a price shock hurts a large economy
Reserves are released in the blockade
Reserves reduce the damage
Lirane's necessities go short in the blockade

title: Prolonged economic crisis followed by gradual recovery
setup: Week 53: Sundara (second-largest economy) loses 35% of all productive capacity and half its stocks, mobilises 6 million workers for two years and takes a -12 stability shock. Mobilisation and the shock end in week 157. Horizon: 20 years.

indicators.label: Weeks to reach 95% / 99% of control GDP
Consumption per head at the end (vs control)
World real GDP at the trough (vs control)

mechanisms: Capacity loss lowers potential output directly; destroyed stocks create immediate shortages, so prices spike and trade partners are drawn in as suppliers.

Unemployment and falling income reduce tax revenue just when relief is needed: deficits and debt rise, the borrowing rate climbs with the debt ratio, and stability drops with unemployment, shortages and the stability shock.

Recovery is gradual because firms rebuild only when the margin on new plant beats the cost of capital, each plant takes about 3-9 months to build, and construction itself needs industrial goods that are scarce after the destruction.
Once mobilisation ends and capacity returns, wages and prices normalise and the autopilot repays debt: the economy converges back to its prior trend without outside help.

checks.name: A deep recession follows the shock
The crisis is prolonged (not a one-quarter blip)
Recovery happens (95% of control GDP within the horizon)
Capacity is rebuilt gradually by private investment
No runaway debt or inflation after the crisis

title: Long-term development with structural change in production and consumption
setup: Thirty years of development of Morvaine (poorest large economy, 80 million people, technology 0.55) under four policy strategies: the autopilot baseline, an infrastructure push (7% of GDP), social-first spending (17% of GDP), and 50% tariffs on industrial, consumer and military goods. All other countries use the autopilot.

indicators.label: Baseline: real GDP per head after 30 years
indicators.note: technology growth, catch-up and capital accumulation

indicators.label: Baseline: food share of household purchases
indicators.note: consumption shifts to manufactures and services as incomes rise (Engel effect)

indicators.label: Baseline: industrial + consumer goods share of output
Baseline: trade openness (first / last two years)
Best strategy for GDP per head

mechanisms: Technology rises with a world trend plus catch-up for zones behind the frontier; infrastructure raises productivity and growth; capital accumulates where margins beat the cost of capital. Poorer zones therefore grow faster than rich ones, narrowing the gap slowly.

Household budgets have a subsistence core (mostly food) and the rest is split by fixed shares: as income rises the food share of spending falls and manufactures and services gain. Output follows demand and comparative advantage, so the production structure shifts without any scripted transition.

The strategies trade off differently: infrastructure raises long-run productivity but costs stability and debt early; social spending buys stability and consumption but slows capital formation; tariffs raise domestic prices and shield local producers at the cost of efficiency and trade partners.

checks.name: Living standards rise over 30 years
Household food share falls as incomes rise
Production structure changes
Several strategies are viable (no strategy collapses)
Strategies differ measurably
Protectionism lowers openness
